summary: Sun Pharma develops and makes finished medicines, supplies ingredients used to make medicines, and sells selected consumer-health products.
description: A tablet, cream or injection is a finished medicine. The active ingredient is the substance inside it that produces its intended effect. Sun Pharma works in both: it supplies finished medicines through healthcare sales channels and ingredients to other medicine makers. It also spends on developing new medicines.
money: Customers pay for medicines, ingredients or work and rights covered by specific agreements. Sun pays for research, testing, ingredients, factories, quality checks, distribution and sales. Developing a medicine can cost money long before permission to sell it is obtained, and some projects do not reach that stage.
customers: Distributors, pharmacies, hospitals and other medicine manufacturers buy different offerings. The patient uses the medicine, but the commercial buyer can be a distributor or hospital. Doctors’ prescribing decisions and the rules of the relevant country also affect which products reach patients.
drivers: Which products actually reach sale, what customers will pay, competition, reliable factory supply, required approvals and the cost of research and selling.

groups.title: Finished medicines
groups.examples: Tablets, creams, injections and other approved forms for skin, eye, heart and other care.
groups.explanation: These are supplied in a form ready for the approved use. Some carry a brand name; others are generic versions of an existing medicine, developed to meet the relevant approval requirements. The company must manufacture and supply them consistently.

groups.title: New and differentiated medicines
groups.examples: Innovative medicines developed by Sun or sold under relevant commercial rights.
groups.explanation: An innovative medicine involves developing or obtaining a different treatment offering. Testing, permissions and reaching buyers can require substantial spending. The right to sell a product may cover particular countries rather than the whole world.

groups.title: Ingredients sold to medicine makers
groups.examples: Active pharmaceutical ingredients, often shortened to APIs.
groups.explanation: Another manufacturer can buy an ingredient and use it to make its finished medicine. The customer is buying an input, not a ready-to-use patient product. This is a different transaction from a pharmacy buying packs of tablets.

groups.title: Consumer-health products
groups.examples: Selected non-prescription and consumer-health offerings in the catalogue.
groups.explanation: These reach consumers through relevant retail channels. The product’s label and local rules determine how it can be sold and described; a familiar brand does not by itself explain how much the business earns.

basics.title: A generic and a new medicine start from different tasks
basics.text: A generic is developed as a version of an existing medicine and must meet the applicable approval standards. A new medicine can require a different programme of research and testing. Both still need manufacturing, buyers and sales that cover their costs.

basics.title: Permission to sell is different from a sale
basics.text: A regulator is the authority that checks whether a medicine can be sold under the applicable rules. Approval does not mean the product is already on shelves, that buyers have ordered it or that its development costs have been recovered.

steps.title: Choose and develop the offering
steps.text: Work on a finished medicine, an ingredient or a product obtained through an agreement with another company.

steps.title: Complete the required checks
steps.text: Carry out technical work and testing, then seek the necessary permissions for the product and country.

steps.title: Make and supply consistent batches
steps.text: Buy inputs, make the product, test its quality and supply it through the relevant distributor or directly to the agreed business customer.

steps.title: Bill, collect and keep supporting supply
steps.text: Receive customer payments while paying factory, research and selling costs. Quality monitoring and other obligations continue after the first sale.

specifics.title: Other suppliers can change a product’s earnings
specifics.text: A successful generic can attract competing versions, putting pressure on prices. New medicines have different research, legal and selling costs. A higher selling price alone does not establish a higher profit.

specifics.title: A factory issue can interrupt the route to a customer
specifics.text: Regulators inspect how medicines are made. A finding may require changes or restrict supply from a particular site or for particular products. Check the actual scope rather than assuming the whole company is affected in the same way.

specifics.title: Research announcements describe work still to be done
specifics.text: A pipeline is the collection of products being developed. A project may need more testing, payments to partners and permission before it can earn sales. Some will fail or sell less than expected.

watch: Which products and countries explain the change?
Different medicine businesses can move in different directions.

Read the company’s discussion of finished medicines, innovative products, ingredients and countries. These views can overlap: a US medicine sale can also be an innovative-product sale, so do not add both as separate sales.
Are approved products actually reaching customers?
Permission to sell does not establish supply or demand.
Check the sale launch, factory supply, actual orders or sales and price competition. Keep applications, approvals and products already selling separate.
Quality problems can interrupt deliveries and add costs.
Read dated company and regulator notices. Identify the affected factory, product and market, the work required to fix the problem and any later official decision.
What must be paid before new medicines earn money?
Testing and reaching buyers can require spending before sales.
Read research costs, development stages and payments promised to partners when agreed conditions are met. Compare management expectations with completed work and actual sales.
Do sales produce cash after business needs?
Unsold stock and unpaid customer bills tie up money.
Compare cash from day-to-day operations with profit, stock and money customers owe. Also read factory investment, purchase-of-business payments and unusual charges before judging what cash is left.
risks: Competition or reliance on important products
New alternatives, changes in what buyers pay for and expiry of product rights can reduce sales.
Inspection findings, recalls or corrective work can interrupt supply and increase costs.
Testing can fail, permission can be delayed or customer demand can be weaker than expected.
Disputes over product rights, product-related claims and payments promised in agreements can add costs.
context: A signed purchase agreement is not yet a combined company

On 27 April 2026, Sun signed an agreement to buy all the shares of another medicine company, Organon & Co., for cash. Sun’s 30 October 2026 results say approvals from most of the required government authorities have been received, a few are still pending, and the two companies continue to operate separately until the deal closes; Sun indicates closing by the January–March 2027 quarter. Meanwhile Sun is already paying advisers, lawyers and lenders for the deal. It reported these costs, together with a US legal settlement, as exceptional items, meaning unusual charges shown separately from regular business. In that quarter, sales grew while reported net profit fell. Keep the signed agreement, the completed purchase and the later combined results as separate stages.
quiz: Does an approved medicine automatically earn back its development costs?
No. It still needs reliable supply, buyers and a selling price that covers its costs. Approval is an important step, not proof of profitable sales.
sources: Organon purchase status and exceptional charges · results filing 30 October 2026

financialNotes.title: Match the profit definition to the period and scope
financialNotes.text: The audited group reports one Pharmaceuticals segment. The table uses revenue from operations and profit attributable to owners, including reported exceptional items. Product, geographical and therapy sales descriptions can overlap; none establishes a separately audited profit for each medicine or therapy.
